extracted.intended_audience: artists, architects, and educated readers of art criticism (students of ornament/architecture)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging grotesque (ornamental) art and architecture: distinguishing noble vs base grotesque; appropriate uses of play and satire in art; and how social/moral character shows in ornament. Aimed at guiding aesthetic evaluation and production of architectural sculpture and decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque composed of ludicrous and fearful elements
rubrics_metrics.description: The grotesque is, in almost all cases, composed of two elements, one ludicrous, the other fearful; as one or the other element prevails, grotesque falls into sportive or terrible branches, though most examples combine both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing or producing grotesque forms, identify and balance the elements of jest/playfulness and fear/terror. Expect combinations rather than pure types; examine separately the legitimate kinds of jest and fearfulness that may be expressed in art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between true (noble) and false (base) grotesque
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a fundamental difference between 'true' or noble grotesque (magnificent condition of fantastic imagination linked to Gothic mind) and the base grotesqueness of late Renaissance sculpture (delight in bestial vice, sneering mockery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess grotesque works for their imaginative nobleness versus mere mockery. True grotesque elevates imagination and can be compatible with sublimity; false grotesque revels in vulgar sarcasm (e.g., leering heads, tongues out) and indicates cultural decline. This distinction is practically important for contemporary taste and moral judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wise play — appropriate playful expression in noble art
rubrics_metrics.description: Playfulness in its highest form is reverent and inseparable from love of God, truth, and humanity; such minds may play yet their art remains essentially serious, with only scattered, trivial ludic elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In major artistic works (painting, church architecture), playful elements must be sparing and integrated with solemnity; a painter must portray the life/history of a character, not a mere momentary jest. Use subtle, reverent grotesque only as accessory to larger, noble purposes (examples: Wordsworth, Plato).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary play — art of the wayside (recreative/artisan grotesque)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who 'play necessarily' — artisans and working people who need recreation — will produce art that is rougher in technical perfection but often interesting in character or satirical fancy; this 'wayside' art is properly called Grotesque and can be noble or inferior depending on the producer's tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value the delight and human sympathy in artisan-produced grotesque; forgive imperfections as marks of recreation. Recognize artisans may wisely choose satire or quaint invention rather than attempt solemn beauty beyond their training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inordinate play — artistic and social degeneration from excessive play
rubrics_metrics.description: When amusement becomes the object of life, it produces inordinate play which injures society and art: work goes undone, false opinions spread, reverence is eroded, and artistic satire becomes destructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works born of inordinate play as socially and morally harmful; be wary of art that makes perpetual jest the end in itself. Critique the loss of reverence and the spread of falsity in such art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of play — sterility and dulness in art
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who do not play at all (dull, morose, or overworked people) are incapable of inventive or enjoyable jest, and produce art lacking joyous imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize lack of playful energy as a defect: art may be technically competent but emotionally barren. Encourage conditions that allow healthy recreation to enrich artistic production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate grotesque by the moral/tone of the makers
rubrics_metrics.description: Grotesque is noble or inferior according to the tone of the minds which produced it — their knowledge, wit, love of truth, and kindness — and by the strength of expression they could impart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging ornament, consider the maker's moral/intellectual character (as evidenced in inscriptions, portraits, or civic dedication); good-hearted, intelligent makers make delightful grotesque even if imperfect; vicious or vain makers produce base grotesque.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural ornament should reflect proper subject (divine vs human honor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sign of decline is churches and facades built to the glory of men instead of the glory of God (e.g., façades devoid of religious symbols, inscriptions that omit God's name), indicating vanity and loss of religious feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence or absence of religious symbols, inscriptions, and references to the divine as an evaluative criterion for ecclesiastical architecture. A façade dominated by commemorations of individuals signals moral and artistic degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire in art must preserve reverence and be used carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: A common error in playful/inordinate minds is want of reverence when approaching important or sacred subjects; careless satire can encourage irreverence in others and destroy the guidance that reverence offers toward truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply satire with caution — avoid exposing weakness to audiences unable to appreciate greatness; ensure satirical elements do not undermine subjects of sanctity or essential truths. Evaluate satire by its conscientiousness and restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of imperfections in recreative 'wayside' art
rubrics_metrics.description: The delightfulness of art produced in recreation (wayside grotesque) consists mainly in the imperfections that mark it as work done in leisure; its chief appeal is to the spectator's sympathy with the maker's enjoyment rather than to technical exactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing such ornament, consider the emotional pleasure and human context of production; forgive technical faults and appreciate the spontaneous charm of the maker's recreation.
